title: AWS Cloud Fundamentals and Global Infrastructure
objectives: Explain cloud computing and the IaaS, PaaS and serverless service models in AWS terms.
Describe Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations and Local Zones and why each exists.
Choose a Region using compliance, latency, service availability and price.
Apply the shared responsibility model to a developer's daily work.
Outline the four DVA-C02 exam domains this 30-day plan follows.
definition: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases and other IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. AWS runs this infrastructure in Regions around the world; each Region contains multiple isolated Availability Zones, and a global network of edge locations brings content closer to users.

theory.heading: Why developers use the cloud
theory.body: Instead of buying servers months in advance, a developer calls an API and receives a database, a queue or a function in seconds. This changes capital expense into variable expense, removes capacity guessing and lets teams experiment cheaply. For the Developer Associate exam the focus is on building with managed services, so you spend time on application logic rather than patching operating systems.
points: IaaS (EC2): you manage the OS, runtime and application.
PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk): AWS manages the platform; you deploy code.
Serverless (Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS): no servers to manage; you pay per request or per use.
Everything in AWS is an API call: the console, CLI, SDKs and CloudFormation all call the same APIs.

theory.heading: Regions and Availability Zones
theory.body: A Region is a separate geographic area, such as ap-south-1 (Mumbai) or ap-south-2 (Hyderabad). Regions are isolated from each other so that a failure in one does not spread. Each Region has multiple Availability Zones (AZs), usually three or more; an AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to the other AZs by low-latency links. Deploying across at least two AZs is the basic pattern for high availability.
points: Most resources are Regional (Lambda, DynamoDB tables, SQS queues) or zonal (an EC2 instance, an EBS volume).
Some services are global: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront and AWS Organizations.
Data does not leave a Region unless you configure replication or transfer it.
AZ names such as ap-south-1a are mapped differently per account; AZ IDs (aps1-az1) are consistent.

theory.heading: Edge locations, Local Zones and Wavelength
theory.body: Edge locations (points of presence) are far more numerous than Regions and are used by CloudFront, Route 53, AWS Global Accelerator and Lambda@Edge to serve users with low latency. Local Zones place selected compute and storage close to large cities, and Wavelength Zones embed AWS inside telecom 5G networks. These exist because the speed of light is a hard limit: a user in Chennai served from us-east-1 sees roughly 200 ms round-trip time.
points: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations close to viewers.
Local Zones suit latency-sensitive workloads such as gaming or media rendering.
Edge locations do not host your general workloads; they cache and route.

theory.heading: Choosing a Region
theory.body: Region choice is a frequent interview question because it shows architectural judgement. The order matters: first legal and compliance requirements (data residency rules may require data to stay in India), then latency to users, then whether the services you need are available in that Region, and finally price, which differs between Regions.
points: Compliance and data residency: non-negotiable, filter first.
Proximity: lower latency to most users.
Service availability: new services and features often launch in a few Regions first.
Pricing: the same service can cost more in one Region than another.

theory.heading: Shared responsibility model
theory.body: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud: physical data centres, hardware, the global network and the virtualisation layer. The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud: IAM permissions, data encryption choices, network configuration and application code. The split moves with the service model: on EC2 you patch the guest OS; on Lambda AWS patches the runtime environment, but your code, dependencies and IAM role remain your job.
points: AWS: facilities, hardware, hypervisor, managed-service infrastructure.
Customer: data, IAM, encryption settings, security groups, application code.
The more managed the service, the less operational work for you.

theory.heading: The DVA-C02 exam at a glance
theory.body: The AWS Certified Developer – Associate exam tests whether you can build, deploy, secure and debug applications on AWS. It has four domains: Development with AWS Services (32%), Security (26%), Deployment (24%) and Troubleshooting and Optimization (18%). Questions are scenario-based, so this course explains why one service or setting fits a situation better than another.
points: 65 questions (50 scored, 15 unscored) in 130 minutes; scaled score 100–1000, pass mark 720.
Multiple-choice and multiple-response questions with no penalty for guessing.

example.title: Inspecting Regions and AZs with the AWS CLI
example.body: Two read-only CLI calls show the infrastructure your account can use. The first lists enabled Regions; the second lists the AZs in Mumbai with their consistent zone IDs. Using --query (JMESPath) and --output table keeps the result readable.

code.source:
aws ec2 describe-regions --query "Regions[].RegionName" --output table

aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region ap-south-1 \
  --query "AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId,State]" --output table

use_cases.title: Data residency for Indian fintech
use_cases.description: A payments start-up keeps customer data in ap-south-1 and ap-south-2 to meet regulatory requirements, using two Regions for disaster recovery inside India.

use_cases.title: Multi-AZ web application
use_cases.description: An application runs behind a load balancer across three AZs so that losing one data centre does not take the site down.

use_cases.title: Global content delivery
use_cases.description: An ed-tech platform serves video lessons through CloudFront edge locations so students across India get low-latency playback.

use_cases.title: Experiments without hardware
use_cases.description: A developer spins up a DynamoDB table and a Lambda function for a prototype, then deletes them the same day and pays only for usage.

demonstration.description: Use the AWS SDK for Python (boto3) to print how many AZs each of two Regions offers. The client is created per Region because most AWS APIs are Regional endpoints. Exact counts depend on your account and when you run it.

code.source:
import boto3

for region in ['ap-south-1', 'ap-south-2']:
    ec2 = boto3.client('ec2', region_name=region)
    zones = ec2.describe_availability_zones()['AvailabilityZones']
    names = [z['ZoneName'] for z in zones if z['State'] == 'available']
    print(region, len(names), names)

takeaways: A Region is an isolated geographic area; an AZ is one or more data centres inside it.
Use at least two AZs for high availability; use multiple Regions for disaster recovery or global users.
Choose a Region by compliance first, then latency, service availability and price.
IAM, Route 53 and CloudFront are global; most other services are Regional.
AWS secures the cloud itself; you secure your data, permissions and code.
Every console click is an API call, which is why the CLI and SDKs can automate everything.

interview.question: What is the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?
interview.answer: A Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones. An AZ is one or more data centres with independent power and networking, connected to other AZs in the same Region by low-latency links.
interview.explanation: Strong answers add the purpose: AZs give fault isolation for high availability within a Region, while multiple Regions give disaster recovery and global reach.

interview.question: How would you choose a Region for a new application?
interview.answer: Filter by compliance and data residency first, then pick the Region with the lowest latency to most users, confirm every required service and feature is available there, and compare pricing.
interview.explanation: Interviewers listen for the order. Compliance is a hard constraint; latency, availability and cost are trade-offs.

interview.question: Explain the shared responsibility model with a Lambda example.
interview.answer: AWS manages the data centres, hardware, operating system and runtime patching for Lambda. The developer is responsible for the function code, its dependencies, the IAM execution role, environment-variable secrets and data encryption choices.
interview.explanation: Using a concrete managed service shows you understand that responsibility shifts with the service model rather than reciting a definition.

interview.question: Which AWS services are global rather than Regional?
interview.answer: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, AWS Organizations and WAF when attached to CloudFront are global. Services such as Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS and S3 buckets are Regional, although S3 has a global namespace for bucket names.
interview.explanation: Mentioning the S3 nuance (global names, Regional buckets) is a common follow-up and shows precision.

interview.question: Your users are in India and Europe and the app must survive a full Region outage. What would you propose?
interview.answer: Deploy in two Regions (for example ap-south-1 and eu-west-1), each across multiple AZs, replicate data with DynamoDB global tables or S3 Cross-Region Replication, and route users with Route 53 latency-based routing plus health checks for failover.
interview.explanation: A strong answer separates AZ-level availability from Region-level disaster recovery and names concrete replication and routing services.

practice.title: Pick the best AWS Region
practice.objective: Apply the Region-selection order used by architects: compliance, required services, latency and then price.
practice.statement: Read the services your application needs, the countries where data is allowed to live, and a list of candidate Regions. A Region is eligible only if its country is allowed (or the allowed list is ANY) and it offers every required service. Among eligible Regions choose the lowest latency; break ties by the lower price index and then by Region name in alphabetical order. Print how many Regions are eligible and the selection.
practice.input_format:
Line 1: required services, comma-separated.
Line 2: allowed country codes, comma-separated, or ANY.
Line 3: n, the number of candidate Regions.
Next n lines: region country latency_ms price_index services (services comma-separated, no spaces).
practice.output_format:
Line 1: Eligible regions: <count>
Line 2: Selected: <region> (latency <ms> ms, price index <price>)
or NO SUITABLE REGION when none is eligible.

example.input:
lambda,dynamodb
IN
4
ap-south-1 IN 18 100 lambda,dynamodb,s3
ap-south-2 IN 25 95 lambda,dynamodb
ap-southeast-1 SG 60 105 lambda,dynamodb,s3
us-east-1 US 210 80 lambda,dynamodb,s3,bedrock
example.output:
Eligible regions: 2
Selected: ap-south-1 (latency 18 ms, price index 100)

constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 50; latency and price index are positive integers.
Country codes are compared in uppercase.
practice.starter:
required = [s.strip().lower() for s in input().split(',') if s.strip()]
allowed = input().strip().upper()
n = int(input())

# TODO: read the n candidates, filter them, then choose by latency, price, name
explanation: Store the required services as a set so a subset check (required <= offered) tests availability in one step.
Apply the hard constraints first: skip Regions in a disallowed country or missing a service.
Keep each eligible Region as a tuple (latency, price, name); Python compares tuples left to right, which is exactly the tie-break order.
min() of the tuples gives the answer; print NO SUITABLE REGION when the list is empty.

quiz.question: What best describes an AWS Availability Zone?
options: A geographic area that contains several Regions
A virtual network you create for your account
A single edge location used by CloudFront
One or more discrete data centres with independent power and networking inside a Region
quiz.explanation: An AZ is one or more isolated data centres within a Region. A VPC is the virtual network; edge locations serve CloudFront.

quiz.question: A healthcare company must keep patient records inside India, and most users are in Bengaluru. What should drive the Region decision first?
options: The Region with the lowest on-demand price
The Region with the most edge locations
The data residency requirement, which limits the choice to Indian Regions
The Region where new services launch first
quiz.explanation: Compliance is a hard constraint and is applied before latency, service availability or price.

quiz.question: Which of these services is global rather than Regional?
options: AWS Lambda
Amazon SQS
IAM
Amazon DynamoDB
quiz.explanation: IAM users, roles and policies are global to the account. DynamoDB tables, Lambda functions and SQS queues live in a specific Region.

quiz.question: Under the shared responsibility model, who patches the operating system that runs your AWS Lambda functions?
options: The developer, through a Lambda layer
The customer's operations team using Systems Manager
Nobody, because Lambda has no operating system
AWS, because Lambda is a managed service
quiz.explanation: For Lambda, AWS manages and patches the underlying OS and managed runtimes. You remain responsible for your code, dependencies and IAM role.

quiz.question: An application must keep running if a single data centre fails, at the lowest extra complexity. What is the standard design?
options: Deploy only to edge locations
Run copies in five Regions with manual failover
Run in a single AZ with larger instances
Deploy across at least two Availability Zones in one Region
quiz.explanation: Multi-AZ deployment within one Region handles the loss of a data centre. Multi-Region is for Region-level disaster recovery and adds more complexity.
